inline.s: Wang Rixiu

He was the Layman Longshu of the Song dynasty, author of the Pure Land Text, who collated and edited the Larger Amitabha Sutra. When the layman was about to pass away, he took leave of all his relatives and old friends, and urged them on in Pure Land practice. Before the end he still recited and lectured with his disciples and paid homage to the Buddha as always, and at death he passed away standing upright.

This book adopts the first view. The reason is that, judged by the essential purport and the thread of meaning of the sutra, it should read: "Therefore, all dharmas spoken by the Tathagata are dharmas of becoming Buddha." Second, the Buddha-dharma spoken of here means the dharma of becoming Buddha. If it were interpreted as "Therefore, the Tathagata says: all dharmas are dharmas of becoming Buddha," then the false teachings of other paths, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct and lying, and so on, would also be dharmas of becoming Buddha; and above all, this assertion (that all dharmas are dharmas of becoming Buddha) risks being abused. Should one not be careful? If, for the sake of greedily enjoying worldly pleasures, one makes the excuse that one "eats yet does not eat" or "acts yet does not act," that is exceedingly dangerous. The Song of Realizing the Way says: "Emptiness unhindered, denying cause and effect, vast and boundless, it invites calamity; the sickness of discarding existence and clinging to emptiness is the same—it is like fleeing drowning only to leap into fire."

Yet, to return to the point: the assertion that "all dharmas are dharmas of becoming Buddha" is, spoken from a deeper level, correct. As the Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "Every form is the Buddha's form; every sound is the Buddha's sound." But one must have awakened to the corresponding ground before one may speak in this way. It is like the general rule that water extinguishes fire: yet if the fire is a raging blaze, the water poured on it is broken down by the high heat into hydrogen and oxygen; hydrogen burns of itself and oxygen feeds the flame, so that the fire blazes even more fiercely. For one who has reached this stage, "the yellow flowers beyond the window are none other than prajna; the green bamboo in the courtyard is all true suchness." If one sees things thus, then every matter can be polished and tempered, every time is practice, everywhere one receives the benefit, and every place is the Buddha-dharma.
[Subhuti! What are called all dharmas are not all dharmas; therefore they are called all dharmas.]

Subhuti! What are called all dharmas (their marks exist), are not all dharmas (their essence is void); therefore they are called all dharmas (they are illusory). This says that all dharmas have marks but no essence; they are illusory.

Considering that there would again be sentient beings who cling to the Buddha-dharma, the World-Honored One admonished further: what the Buddha speaks of as all dharmas is illusory. Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have clung either to existence or to nonexistence; this is a habitual tendency formed over life after life, extremely stubborn. That is why the World-Honored One says again and again in this sutra: it is not existence, not nonexistence, but illusion.
Compare Section Eight: "Subhuti! What are called Buddha and dharma are not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma."
[Subhuti! Suppose a person's body is great and tall. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! When the Tathagata speaks of a body great and tall, it is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body.]

Subhuti! Suppose a person's body is great and tall. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! When the Tathagata speaks of a body great and tall (its marks exist), it is not a great body (its essence is void); therefore it is called a great body (it is illusory).

In Section Ten there is this passage: "Subhuti! Suppose there were a person whose body were like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains. What do you think—would that body be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? The Buddha says it is not a body; therefore it is called a great body." Here the World-Honored One had taught the principle of the purified mind ("one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on form, nor give rise to the mind dwelling on sound, fragrance, taste, touch or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that dwells on nothing whatsoever"), and then tossed out this topic of the wondrous reward body, in which cultivators take such keen interest, to see how well Subhuti had grasped and mastered this principle of the purified mind. Subhuti's first sentence, "Very great," was like a mirror reflecting an object—that was right; his second sentence said at once that this body is an illusion, tightly guarding the original mind and not being dragged along by circumstances. This shows that the Venerable Subhuti had not only grasped the principle of the purified mind but applied it very well, setting us an example: every thought abides in the Way. Now the World-Honored One said again: "Subhuti! Suppose a person's body is great and tall." And so Subhuti said at once: "World-Honored One! When the Tathagata speaks of a body great and tall, it is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body." This is the example of tightly guarding the original mind and not being dragged along by circumstances.

[Subhuti! Bodhisattvas are likewise. If one should say, I shall liberate countless sentient beings, then one is not called a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma called bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life span.]

Subhuti! The great body is an illusion, and the bodhisattva is likewise an illusion. If a bodhisattva thinks, I shall liberate countless sentient beings, then he is not a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! In truth, there is no such thing as a bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says there is no such dharma as self, person, sentient being or life span.

[If one should say, I shall liberate countless sentient beings, then one is not called a bodhisattva] In liberating sentient beings a bodhisattva must not cling to marks. "If one should say, I shall liberate countless sentient beings"—this is clinging to marks. Cultivation means turning delusion into awakening, and clinging to marks is delusion; hence cultivation that clings to marks cannot succeed—as the saying goes, boiling sand will not make rice. Therefore one who practices the six paramitas while clinging to marks is not called a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva should say: I shall liberate countless sentient beings, and yet in truth no sentient being attains liberation. [In truth there is no dharma called bodhisattva] In truth there is no such thing as "called bodhisattva." This says that the bodhisattva is an illusion and not truly existent; it echoes the passage above, "in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi." [The Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life span] This says that there is no such thing at all as self, person, sentient being or life span; they are all illusions.

[Subhuti! If a bodhisattva should say, I shall adorn the Buddha lands, then he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as adorning the Buddha lands is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self, the Tathagata calls him a true bodhisattva.]

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva thinks, I shall adorn the Buddha lands, then he is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this said? Because adorning the Buddha lands is an illusion, and to take an illusion as real (I shall adorn the Buddha lands) is therefore not a bodhisattva. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self (no self of person, no self of dharmas), such a bodhisattva the Tathagata calls a true bodhisattva. (See Section Ten, Adorning the Pure Land: "Subhuti! What do you think—does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha lands? No, World-Honored One! Why? What is called adorning the Buddha lands is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning.")

Since there is no such thing as self, person, sentient being or life span, a bodhisattva practicing the six paramitas and all practices to adorn the Buddha lands must likewise not cling to marks. Only one who comprehends the dharma of no-self is truly a bodhisattva.

Above it was said that body and mind are illusory; now it is said that becoming Buddha is illusory, that self, person, sentient being and life span are illusory, and that a bodhisattva's cultivation and adorning of the Buddha lands is likewise illusory. Then who is it that cultivates? And how does one cultivate?
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, Bodhisattva Samantabhadra raised precisely this question:

"World-Honored One, if those sentient beings know that all is like an illusion, and that body and mind are likewise illusory, how can they use illusion to cultivate what is illusory? If all illusory natures are utterly extinguished, there is then no mind—who is it that cultivates? And why further speak of cultivation as illusory? If those sentient beings do not cultivate at all, they will forever dwell in illusory transformation within birth and death, never understanding the realm that is like an illusion; how then can their deluded minds be liberated? We pray you to tell us, for the sake of all sentient beings of the final age, what skillful means and gradual stages of practice will enable all sentient beings forever to leave behind all illusions."
The World-Honored One gave this teaching in reply:

"Good man! The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathagata's wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, just as flowers in the sky come into being from the sky: though the illusory flowers perish, the nature of the sky is not destroyed. The illusory minds of sentient beings are still extinguished in dependence on illusion; when all illusions are utterly extinguished, the mind of enlightenment does not move. To speak of enlightenment in dependence on illusion is also called illusion; if one says there is enlightenment, one has not yet left illusion, and to say there is no enlightenment is likewise so. Therefore the extinction of illusion is called unmoving.

"Good man, all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should keep far away from all illusory and false realms; because of firmly holding to the mind that keeps far away, the mind that is like an illusion is likewise kept far away; the keeping far away is itself illusion and is likewise kept far away; the illusion of keeping far away from keeping far away is likewise kept far away; when one reaches having nothing left to keep away from, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks rub against each other, fire comes forth and the wood is consumed, and the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished; cultivating the illusory with the illusory is likewise so: when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation
(it is not that everything becomes nothing, but that the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment shines forth clearly).

"Good man! Knowing illusion, one at once leaves it, without resorting to skillful means; leaving illusion is itself enlightenment, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who cultivate in accordance with this will thus be able forever to leave behind all illusions.

"At that time the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this meaning again, spoke in verse: Samantabhadra, you should know, all sentient beings without exception, their beginningless illusory ignorance, all is established from the Tathagata's mind of perfect enlightenment; like flowers in empty space, which depend on space and have marks. If the sky flowers perish again, empty space itself does not move. Illusion is born from the various enlightenments; when illusion is extinguished, enlightenment is complete, because the mind of enlightenment does not move. If those bodhisattvas, and sentient beings of the final age, always keep far from illusion, all illusions are wholly left behind. As fire is born from wood, and when the wood is consumed the fire is extinguished, so enlightenment admits no gradual stages, and skillful means are likewise so."
(For detailed annotations, see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

blocks.text: One Essence, Equally Contemplated, Chapter Eighteen

inline.s: This section uses the five eyes to show the perfection and harmony of the Buddha's vision, which contemplates all equally and, amid apparent birth and death, sees only the unborn. Hence its title, One Essence, Equally Contemplated.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the physical eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the physical eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the physical eye.
[Physical eye] The physical eye is the eye of an ordinary being in a physical body; when it meets darkness or an obstruction, it cannot see.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the heavenly eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the heavenly eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the heavenly eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the heavenly eye.
[Heavenly eye] The heavenly eye is the eye of heavenly beings; near and far, by day and by night, it can see all.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the wisdom eye.

[Wisdom eye] The wisdom eye is the eye of the sravaka; it can see through false marks and recognize true emptiness. [True emptiness] The state beyond all marks of form and consciousness, that is, the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the dharma eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the dharma eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the dharma eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the dharma eye.
[Dharma eye] The dharma eye is the eye of the bodhisattva; it can thoroughly understand all dharma gates both worldly and world-transcending.
[Subhuti! What do you think—does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.]
The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? Subhuti replied: yes, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.

[Buddha eye] The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathagata; having the Buddha eye, one also possesses the four eyes that precede it, and can know all things and see all things. Amid all dharmas the Buddha eye constantly illumines.

The next passage says that the Tathagata has these five eyes (physical, heavenly, wisdom, dharma and Buddha eye), knows all and sees all; therefore what the Tathagata speaks is all true words seen with his own eyes.

[Subhuti, what do you think—are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River spoken of by the Buddha as sand? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata speaks of them as sand. Subhuti! What do you think—if there were as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and as many Buddha worlds as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be many? Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: in all those lands, the various minds of all the sentient beings therein are all known to the Tathagata.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River spoken of by the Buddha as sand? Subhuti replied: so it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata speaks of them as sand. The Buddha asked Subhuti: what do you think—if each grain of sand in the Ganges River were one Ganges River, and there were as many Buddha worlds as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers, would that not be very many? Subhuti replied: exceedingly many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: in all those lands of yours (that is, in the trichiliocosm multiplied by the grains of sand of the Ganges, and multiplied again), the various minds (thoughts) of all the sentient beings therein are fully known to the Tathagata.

[Mind] The "mind" here means the deluded mind, that is, thoughts. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes east for west and south for north, falsely taking the four elements as the marks of their own body, and the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects as the marks of their own mind." [Shadowy reflections of the six sense objects] These are the images that arise in dependence on the six sense objects, that is, the thoughts that arise when the six sense faculties meet the six sense objects. [In all those lands of yours] This refers to "as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in one Ganges River, and as many Buddha worlds as the grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers"; that is, the trichiliocosm multiplied by the grains of sand of the Ganges, and multiplied again.
[Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as all minds are all not minds; therefore they are called minds.]

Why does the Tathagata fully know all these countless minds? Because what the Tathagata speaks of as all minds (their marks exist) are all not minds (their essence is void); therefore they are called minds (they are illusory).

[All minds] That is, what the passage above calls "the various minds of all sentient beings." [What the Tathagata speaks of as all minds are all not minds; therefore they are called minds] This says that the minds of all sentient beings are illusory. The Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra

Chapter Eleven on the Illusory Learning says: "Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, perception, formations and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One." Thus we know that body and mind are illusory.

This passage says: why does the Tathagata know all these countless minds? Because they are deluded minds in which thoughts flow on and change; they are illusions, and illusions have marks (modern science and technology can already measure and record the brain waves produced by the activity of thought), and therefore the Tathagata knows them all.

When ordinary people give rise to a thought, even ghosts and spirits know it, how much more the Tathagata. In the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang, a bhikshu came from the West whom people called Great-Ear Tripitaka; he claimed to have the penetration of knowing others' minds (the spiritual power to know the thoughts of other people). Suzong asked National Master Huizhong of Nanyang to test him. The master sat for a while and then asked: where is this old monk's mind? He answered: at Western Sichuan, watching a boat race. After a while the master asked again: where is this old monk's mind? He answered: on the Tianjin Bridge, watching a monkey show. The master then became utterly still, and after a while asked again: where is this old monk's mind? Great-Ear Tripitaka could not answer even after a long time, because the master's thoughts had come to rest, quiescent and without marks.
[What is the reason? Subhuti! The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped.]

Why are they said to be illusions? Because the past mind, the present mind and the future mind are all shadowy reflections of the six sense objects, arising from the objects and ceasing when the objects cease (cannot be grasped); therefore they have no essence to speak of.

The Sutra of the Great Vehicle's Contemplation of the Mind Ground of Original Birth says: "All mind-dharmas of the three periods have emptiness as their intrinsic nature." The three minds are what dwells and the six sense objects are that on which they dwell; both what dwells and that on which it dwells are illusions, all ungraspable. Therefore one must certainly see through and let go: see through that all marks whatsoever are false and unreal, and let go of clinging, discrimination and deluded thinking.
[Three periods] Past, present and future.

blocks.text: Pervading Transformation Throughout the Dharma Realm, Chapter Nineteen

inline.s: Above it was said that the three minds are illusory; this section says that merit and virtue are illusory. "Pervading transformation throughout the dharma realm" means: if one realizes that merit and virtue are illusory and thereupon practices markless giving, one's giving and transformation pervade the dharma realm. This is what Section Four, Wondrous Practice Without Dwelling, says: "Subhuti! What do you think—can the space in the east be measured? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! Can the space in the south, west and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below, be measured? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! When a bodhisattva gives without dwelling on marks, the merit and virtue are likewise so, beyond measure."

[Subhuti! What do you think—if someone filled the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away, would that person, by this cause and condition, obtain much merit? So it is, World-Honored One! That person, by this cause and condition, would obtain very much merit.]

Subhuti! What do you think—if someone took the seven treasures filling the trichiliocosm and gave them away, would that person, by this cause and condition, obtain much merit? Subhuti replied: so it is, World-Honored One! That person, by this cause and condition, obtains very much merit.

[Subhuti! If merit and virtue were real, the Tathagata would not say that the merit and virtue obtained are much; because merit and virtue are not [real], the Tathagata says that the merit and virtue obtained are much.]

Subhuti! If merit and virtue were real (truly existing), the Tathagata would not say that the merit and virtue obtained are much; because merit and virtue are not real (not truly existing), the Tathagata says that the merit and virtue obtained are much.

The World-Honored One explains again: only because merit and virtue are illusory is there any "much" to speak of. Compare Section Eight: "Subhuti! What do you think—if a person filled the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gave them away, would the merit and virtue that person obtains be much? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? This merit and virtue is not the nature of merit and virtue; therefore the Tathagata says the merit and virtue is much." In Section Eight it is Subhuti who says that only because merit and virtue are illusory is there any "much" to speak of; here it is the World-Honored One who says that only because merit and virtue are illusory is there any "much" to speak of.

blocks.text: Leaving Form, Leaving Marks, Chapter Twenty

inline.s: This section says that the Buddha's perfect form body is an illusion, and that the Buddha's thirty-two marks of a great being and eighty subsidiary marks are likewise illusions. "Leaving form, leaving marks" means that the Buddha's perfect form body and the thirty-two marks of a great being with the eighty subsidiary marks can all alike not be clung to as real.

[Subhuti! What do you think—can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect form body? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect form body. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the perfect form body is not the perfect form body; therefore it is called the perfect form body.]

Subhuti! What do you think—can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect form body? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect form body. Why? Because the perfect form body is an illusion—what the Tathagata speaks of as the perfect form body (its marks exist) is not the perfect form body (its essence is void); therefore it is called the perfect form body (it is illusory).
[Perfect form body] The perfected form body.

The perfected form body has marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and unreal; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of it. The sutra says: "If one sees all marks as not marks, one then sees the Tathagata."

[Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by means of the perfect marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the marks being perfect is not perfection; therefore it is called the marks being perfect.]

Subhuti! What do you think—can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfect marks? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen by means of the perfect marks. Why? Because perfection itself is likewise an illusion—what the Tathagata speaks of as the perfection of marks (their marks exist) is not perfection (its essence is void); therefore it is called the perfection of marks (it is illusory).

[Perfect marks] The thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty subsidiary marks that the Buddha's form body possesses. Among the surpassing features and shapes possessed by the Buddha's form body, those that are conspicuous and easily seen are thirty-two in number and are called the thirty-two marks of a great being (the thirty-two marks for short); those that are subtle, hidden and hard to see are eighty in number and are called the eighty subsidiary marks. A wheel-turning sage king likewise possesses the thirty-two marks, but does not possess the eighty subsidiary marks.

The thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty subsidiary marks" have marks, and all marks whatsoever are false and unreal; therefore the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of them. The sutra says: "If one sees all marks as not marks, one then sees the Tathagata."

Compare: Section Five, Seeing the Truth in Accord with Reality: "Subhuti! What do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by means of bodily marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of bodily marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as bodily marks is not bodily marks." Section Thirteen, Upholding the Dharma in Accord with the Dharma: "Subhuti, what do you think—can the Tathagata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why? What the Tathagata speaks of as the thirty-two marks is not marks; therefore it is called the thirty-two marks."

blocks.text: Non-Teaching and What Is Taught, Chapter Twenty-One

inline.s: Non-teaching and what is taught—one who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma.

[Subhuti! Do not say that the Tathagata thinks, I should teach a dharma. Do not think so! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata teaches a dharma, he slanders the Buddha, because he cannot understand what I teach.]

Subhuti! Do not think that the Tathagata has such a thought: I should teach some dharma. Do not think so! Why? If a person says that the Tathagata has the thought that he is teaching the dharma, that person slanders the Buddha, because he cannot understand what my teaching of the dharma really is. (The Buddha teaches while leaving marks: he teaches yet does not teach.)

The Tathagata does not teach by forming a thought (the Tathagata has no thought that he should teach the dharma, nor any thought that he is now teaching the dharma or has already taught it); rather, he responds to conditions and brings forth function, flowing forth naturally from the intrinsic nature. The Tathagata does not cling to the mark of teaching the dharma: he teaches yet does not teach. As it is said, "How does one expound it for others? Not grasping marks, thusness unmoving." (See Section Thirty-Two, Response and Transformation Are Not Real.) Moreover, this very matter of the Tathagata's teaching the dharma is not truly existent; in truth there is no dharma called teaching the dharma. (For "the Tathagata has not taught anything," see Section Thirteen, Upholding the Dharma in Accord with the Dharma: "Subhuti! What do you think—has the Tathagata taught a dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has not taught anything.")
[Subhuti! One who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma.]
Subhuti! One who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught—this is truly teaching the dharma.

The meaning is that one who teaches while clinging to the mark of teaching the dharma (conditioned dharmas) cannot speak of the path of liberation (unconditioned dharma), because he himself has not realized it and does not uphold it. Therefore at the close of this sutra the World-Honored One admonishes: "How does one expound it for others? Not grasping marks, thusness unmoving." (Section Thirty-Two, Response and Transformation Are Not Real.) At the same time, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings is itself already perfect and no different from that of the Buddhas; in this respect there is truly no dharma that can be taught, no practice that can be cultivated, no fruit that can be realized. The problem is that the Buddhas have awakened and have verified their intrinsic nature, while we are still in a dream of delusion and must cultivate and realize before we can awaken. In this respect there is a dharma that must be taught, a practice that must be cultivated, a fruit that must be realized. Yet these dharmas, practices and fruits all proceed within the dream of ignorance; though it is using illusion to leave illusion, it is after all illusion, and illusion is not real. A cultivator must certainly not cling to marks. Hence it is said: no dharma can be taught, no practice can be cultivated, no fruit can be realized.

Master Hanshan says: sentient beings "merely because of beginningless ignorance, which obscures for them the wondrous brightness, give rise to all manner of inversions, deluded thinking and discrimination, and create all manner of karma. It is like a waking person who has nothing to do, yet suddenly in sleep dreams all kinds of dreams, and in the dream the affairs of suffering and joy appear vividly before him; when he wakes and seeks for them, they cannot be found at all. This is called producing something out of nothing—how could it be a real dharma? But deluded people, being inverted, cling to it as truly existent; this is because their seeing is not thorough. When the Buddha appeared in the world and taught all manner of dharmas, these were merely tools for shattering the dream, and had no root either. Yet students of the Buddha-dharma cling to them as dharmas that they themselves truly possess—this is adding dream upon dream." (Dream Roam Collection
Instructions to the Chan Monk Tanyan Zong)

The Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "The Buddha has three bodies: the dharma body teaches the dharma of the intrinsically empty and penetrating nature, the reward body teaches all pure dharmas, and the transformation body teaches the dharma of the six paramitas and all practices. When the dharma body teaches the dharma, it cannot be sought through words, sounds, forms or letters; there is nothing taught and nothing realized—the intrinsic nature is simply empty and penetrating. Hence it is said: 'No dharma can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma.' The reward body and the transformation body both appear in response to the perceptions of beings, and the dharmas they teach likewise follow the matter and respond to the faculties in order to gather and transform; none of them is the true dharma. Hence it is said: the reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they teachers of the dharma."

Master Baojing says: "Now, the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words; the ground of actual principle is originally without anything taught. As it is said, the Way is originally without words, the dharma is originally without teaching. As the Diamond Sutra says: if one says the Tathagata teaches a dharma, that is to slander the Buddha. Why then does the Buddha have a dharma that can be taught? You should know that the Way is originally without words, and words are borrowed to reveal the Way; the dharma is originally without teaching, and teaching is used to reveal the dharma. If one clings to its being inexpressible, one falls into the other paths' view of cutting off speech; if one clings to its being expressible, one incurs the reproach of slandering the Buddha. If one understands that teaching is no teaching, then there is no harm in teaching without teaching. That is why the World-Honored One, teaching the dharma for forty-nine years, never spoke a single word; and though he never spoke a single word, he spoke sideways and upright, blazing forth in unbroken teaching without end. The wonder of the Buddha-dharma lies precisely in this." (Record of Personal Hearing on the Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra)
[At that time the wise-life Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Are there many sentient beings in future ages who, hearing this dharma, will give rise to faith?]
At that time the wise-life Subhuti reverently said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Will the many sentient beings in future ages who hear you speak in this way believe it?
[Wise life] To take wisdom as one's life. Subhuti was foremost in understanding emptiness; taking wisdom as his life, he is called wise-life Subhuti.

The passage above says: "If a person says that the Tathagata teaches a dharma, he slanders the Buddha... one who teaches the dharma has no dharma that can be taught; therefore it is called teaching the dharma." Subhuti was afraid that sentient beings would find this hard to understand, and so asked: in future ages, when they hear you speak in this way, will there be sentient beings who believe it?

[The Buddha said: Subhuti! They are not sentient beings, and yet not non-sentient beings. Why? Subhuti! Sentient beings, sentient beings—the Tathagata says they are not sentient beings; therefore they are called sentient beings.]

The Buddha told Subhuti: Subhuti! They are not sentient beings, and yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why? Subhuti! Because sentient beings are merely illusions (sentient beings, sentient beings—the Tathagata says they are not sentient beings; therefore they are called sentient beings), and yet their intrinsic nature is equal to the Buddha's: they are all-knowing and all-capable, and so are fully able to give rise to faith in this.
[Sentient beings, sentient beings] By the emphatic tone of repetition, this carries on the passage above, "they are not sentient beings, and yet not non-sentient beings."

blocks.text: No Dharma Can Be Attained, Chapter Twenty-Two

inline.s: The preceding section said that the Tathagata has no dharma that can be taught; this section says that the Tathagata has no dharma that can be attained.
[Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Is it that the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and yet there was nothing attained?]
Subhuti reverently said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Is it that the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and yet there was nothing attained?
[The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! As to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, there is not even a single dharma that can be attained; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

The Buddha replied: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! Not only is there nothing to be attained with respect to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—there is not even the slightest dharma that I attain; it is by leaving behind all marks that it is called supreme perfect enlightenment.

Compare Section Seven, No Attainment and No Teaching: "Subhuti! What do you think—has the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Has the Tathagata taught any dharma? Subhuti said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha teaches, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathagata can teach." Section Seventeen, Utterly Without Self: "Subhuti! What do you think—when the Tathagata was with the Buddha Dipankara, did he attain any dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha teaches, when the Buddha was with Dipankara, he had no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. The Buddha said: So it is, so it is. Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara would not have given me the prediction: in a future age you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni. Because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, Dipankara gave me the prediction, saying: in a future age you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni. Why? The Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. If someone says that the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi—Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by the Tathagata is neither real nor unreal therein."

Cultivation without cultivation, realization without realization—this has two meanings. First, why cultivate and why realize? The purpose is to wake from the dream of ignorance. Therefore one must cultivate while leaving marks and realize while leaving marks in order to leave illusion; hence to cultivate without cultivating and to realize without realizing is the true path. Second, fundamentally speaking, cultivation and realization are both matters within the dream of ignorance; there is no truly existing cultivation or realization, and so it is said to be no cultivation and no realization. Even so, one still must cultivate and realize in order to wake from the dream of ignorance—but one must certainly cultivate while leaving marks and realize while leaving marks.
That the World-Honored One taught no dharma and attained no anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is truly hard to believe, and so the sutra speaks of these two matters again and again.

Speaking of how all dharmas are like the realm of illusion and dream, Master Hanshan says: "All Buddhas appear by the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate by the power of illusion; all followers of the Two Vehicles hasten to quiescence by the power of illusion; all followers of other paths are stupefied by the power of illusion; all sentient beings are born and die by the power of illusion; and as for the heavenly palaces and Pure Lands, they are established by the power of illusion; the jewel groves and precious trees flourish by the power of illusion; the iron bed and copper pillar are set up by the power of illusion; the cauldron of boiling water and the brazier of coals seethe by the power of illusion; the scaled, the shelled, the feathered and the furred fly and dive by the power of illusion; the wriggling worms and the creeping things move and rest by the power of illusion—so that all that the Buddhas of the three periods have realized and all that the patriarchs of the six generations have transmitted never goes beyond this net of illusion." (See Dream Roam Collection
Instructions to the Chan Monk Zhenyu)

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: "Good man, when bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who cultivate and master this mind reach the state in which there is no cultivation and no attainment, perfect enlightenment illumines everywhere, quiescent and without duality; within it, the hundreds of thousands of millions of asankhyeyas of inexpressible Ganges-sand Buddha worlds are like flowers in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion, neither identical nor separate, neither bound nor freed. Only then does one know that sentient beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth and death and nirvana are like a dream of yesterday."

Master Hanshan comments: this explains again the mark of perfect enlightenment illumining everywhere, quiescent and without duality, in order to reveal the ultimate realization of the one mind in its entirety. For in the tathagata-garbha there is originally no mark of delusion or awakening, of birth or death, of coming or going. Yet birth and death and nirvana are all matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is shattered, looking back on past affairs, they are like a dream of yesterday.

blocks.text: Purified Mind, Practicing Good, Chapter Twenty-Three

inline.s: Purified mind means the pure mind free of discrimination and clinging. The sutra text of this section says: "With no self, no person, no sentient being and no life span, cultivate all good dharmas, and you will attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi." Hence the title of this section: Purified Mind, Practicing Good.

[Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. With no self, no person, no sentient being and no life span, cultivate all good dharmas, and you will attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]
Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

—Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma (referring to the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi spoken of above) regards all things with equality, because one truly understands that they are all illusions; therefore there is no discrimination of high and low, noble and base, right and wrong, defiled and pure, and so on. That is why it is called supreme perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-sambodhi).
Tang
Xuanzang's translation: "Furthermore, Subhuti! This dharma is equal; within it there is nothing unequal. Therefore it is called supreme perfect bodhi."

This sentence says: what is supreme perfect enlightenment? Supreme perfect enlightenment is the total relinquishing of all discrimination and clinging—this is the Buddha, and this is the dharma attained by the Buddha.
This dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi" has several meanings as follows:
1. Any sentient being whatsoever can realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

2. Whichever path one takes, and whether the time is short or long, so long as one awakens completely, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. For the one who realizes it, there is no high or low, no new or old, no shallow or deep.
3. The dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi regards all things with equality.
Why is there discrimination and clinging? Because one takes illusions as real! Thus one clings to marks and grasps at objects, and so there is turning about.

The Essential Teachings on the Transmission of Mind says: "Students of the Way today do not awaken within their own minds, but outside the mind cling to marks and grasp at objects, all of which is contrary to the Way. As for the Ganges sand: the Buddha says it is sand (the Buddha speaks of this sand); when all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, Shakra, Brahma and the heavenly hosts walk across it, the sand is not pleased; when oxen, sheep, insects and ants trample over it, the sand is not angry; with precious gems and fragrant perfumes, the sand is not greedy; with filth, urine and stench, the sand is not averse. This mind is the mind of no-mind (not grasping marks, regarding all with equality). Leaving all marks, there is no further difference between sentient beings and Buddhas; if one can simply be without mind (free of discrimination and clinging), that is the ultimate. If a student of the Way does not directly become mindless, then even kalpas of cultivation will in the end not accomplish the Way; bound by the practices of the Three Vehicles, one will not attain liberation."

[Three Vehicles] "Vehicle" means a conveyance; here it is a metaphor for the dharma gates that carry sentient beings across birth and death to the other shore of nirvana. In accordance with the dull, middling and keen faculties of sentient beings, the Buddha correspondingly taught the three teachings of the sravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle and the bodhisattva vehicle. The Three Vehicles are the Lesser Vehicle, the Middle Vehicle and the Great Vehicle. The Lesser Vehicle is the sravaka vehicle, the Middle Vehicle the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Great Vehicle the bodhisattva vehicle.

The World-Honored One teaches again and again with earnest instructions throughout this sutra, precisely so that we may awaken from the dream of delusion and no longer discriminate or cling. Love and hate, taking and rejecting, greed, anger, delusion and arrogance are the root of birth and death; they must be removed before birth and death can be ended. Therefore one must put great effort into removing discrimination and clinging from the mind.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, in its Verse on No Direction, says:
Those who truly walk the Way discern no fault in the world;
If you see others' faults, your own fault is the worse;
Their fault is not my fault, but my fault is truly mine;
Only cast off the fault-finding mind and shatter your afflictions;
With hate and love unminded, stretch out both legs and lie at ease.
